## What Lasts

In the muddy soil of Novgorod, in the northwest of Russia, the water table sits high and the air cannot reach down. That accident of geology preserved a medieval city's underside — streets of layered timber, combs, toys, and thousands of small sheets of birch bark covered in writing. Bark was the poor man's paper, cheap enough to scribble on and throw away, which is precisely why almost none was ever meant to last.

Among the bark scrolls pulled from the mud is a handful belonging to a boy named Onfim. He was six or seven years old. Around 1240 or so, he sat through lessons and practiced his letters in the usual tedious way — rows of the alphabet, syllables repeated until they dissolved into pure sound. Then, when the tedium won, he drew. There is a picture of a little figure on a horse with a lance; pictures of warriors; and one drawing of a snarling animal that Onfim identified with himself in a label beside it, words to the effect of *I am a wild beast*. Under an alphabet exercise he wrote, neatly, a small prayer asking God to help his servant Onfim.

Seven hundred and eighty years later, those prayers and homework assignments are among the most beloved objects in Russian archaeology. Scholars have learned to recognize his handwriting the way you'd recognize a nephew's. Here is everything we will ever know about Onfim: his name, his letters, his doodles, his self-portrait as a monster, and one glimpse of a teacher's discipline — part of a scroll shows a fir cone drawn over a boy's head, presumably punishment for fidgeting. That's all. And it is, strangely, a kind of abundance.

* * *

Here is the thing nobody tells you about posterity: it does not read monuments. Posterity rummages. It lifts the lids of trash heaps, sifts latrines, unpicks the bindings of old books, x-rays mummy wrappings. It collects parking tickets, shopping lists, tavern debts, onionskins of cargo manifests. We spend enormous energy building things designed to be remembered — pyramids, triumphal arches, statues on horses — and posterity, if it notices them at all, usually uses them for target practice, quarries, or urban fill. The things that actually speak across centuries tend to be the things that were thrown away without a second thought. Posthumous fame goes to the receipts.

Consider a Roman fort called Vindolanda, just south of what became Hadrian's Wall. Around the year 100, officers and their families lived there in damp provincial discomfort, and they wrote constantly — on thin leaves of wood, pen and ink, day after day. Letter after letter accumulated and sank into oxygen-starved mud, where the ink simply stopped happening and waited. Two thousand years later the site began yielding them by the bushel, and they turn out to contain approximately nothing glorious. One resident ordered goods shipped north, grumbling about shipment delays. Someone tallied deliveries of barley and casks of beer. A soldier asked relatives to send socks and underpants, please, immediately, it is cold up here. Somebody kept what amounts to a laundry roster.

And then there is the single most famous tablet from the site: an invitation from Claudia Severa to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of another officer, asking her to come celebrate Claudia Severa's birthday on a September morning. The body of the letter was written by a professional scribe, but at the bottom, in a different, less practiced hand, Claudia Severa added a postscript herself — affectionate phrases, a personal flourish, *farewell, my sister, my dearest soul*. From the entire landscape of Roman Britain, most of it silent, we hear one woman telling her friend not to forget her birthday party. Historians of women's literacy treat that page with the reverence other people reserve for treaty archives, because original handwriting by Roman women survives almost nowhere else. Monumental history gave us legions, frontiers, governors' names. The mud gave us a friendship.

* * *

When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE it did something very similar to a whole city's casual chatter: it shellacked the walls. Pompeians wrote on walls the way we post online, compulsively and anonymously, and the ash kept copies. Political sloganeering is everywhere —竞选 posters urging neighbors to vote for candidates with platform promises of free shows and bread. There are advertisements for gladiatorial matches promising quantities of combatants and adequate shade. There are bar tabs chalked into permanence, customers owing the innkeeper various sums, and insults traded between shopkeepers.

But the graffiti that stops visitors cold is the private stuff. People declaring love in rough Latin, naming their beloveds. Two friends signing *we two, steadfast companions, were here* — and adding, magnificently, *if you want to know our names, ask the walls*, apparently forgetting that no wall can answer. And one anonymous wit who stepped back, surveyed a surface densely covered by generations of passers-by, and wrote the eternal complaint: *I wonder, wall, that you haven't already collapsed under the weight of so much scribbling.* That sentence has now been read by millions of people. Its author wanted, probably, to be cleverer than other pedestrians. Instead he became immortal by complaining about immortality-seeking, which might be the most human outcome imaginable.

* * *

There is a pattern underneath all of this, and once you see it, you cannot stop seeing it. Destruction follows intention like a loyal dog. Bronze is precious — melt it, always. Gold tempts every generation of thieves within reach. Marble gets burned in kilns to make lime mortar; dressed stone gets carted off to whatever fortification needs foundations nearby. The Colossus of Rhodes fell in an earthquake and, legend says, was hauled away on nine hundred camels by a scrap dealer. The Parthenon was intact for two thousand years until somebody stored gunpowder in it, and a Venetian mortar round proved the stones were indeed reusable. Statues with faces outlast invasions only to meet weather or iconoclasm. Anything built to be looked at forever attracts people with hammers.

Meanwhile, in the pits and dumps, the cheapest objects sit inert in the dark with nothing anyone wants, surviving by famine of interest. The daintiest and least durable-seeming things endure absurdly well under the right chemical luck: leather shoes, straw, textiles, fingerprints pressed into clay sealing-stems, dinner leftovers. Archaeologists working sites like Vindolanda recover combs, tent pegs, wooden toy swords, still-flexible sandal straps. Entropy does not take everything equally. It takes what matters.

So preservation on the timescale of millennia is mostly an act of neglect. The best repository for your writing turns out to be a landfill in a dry desert. The surest way to doom your work for eternity is to store it somewhere important.

* * *

Sometimes even carelessness becomes a masterpiece. In Tanzania, at a place called Laetoli, volcanic ash from a nearby eruption fell damp onto the savanna some 3.66 million years ago, and creatures walked across it before the sun dried it into a yielding paste — including, as we found in the 1970s, at least three hominins traveling in a loose procession, two of the smaller ones possibly dutifully stepping into the larger one's prints. Their bones have vanished entirely. Nothing remains of the walkers themselves, not a tooth. What remains is pressure: evenly spaced impressions of feet whose big toes point forward instead of out, meaning they walked upright, strolling on already-modern legs while their ancestors' brains were still far ahead in the future. It may be the oldest footprint trail of our lineage anywhere on Earth, produced by absolutely no one intending to say anything. It says everything available: *someone walked here, with company, unhurried.*

* * *

At the opposite extreme of human time stands Oxyrhynchus, a modest Greco-Egyptian town whose outskirts held a mountainous garbage dump that went largely unused once people stopped living the old way. In 1896 two young Oxford classicists, Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, started digging into it, reasoning sensibly that a town dump beats a tomb for volume of paper. They were right beyond dreaming. Dry Egyptian air had mummified an entire civilization's paperwork: private letters, school exercises, tax assessments, horoscopes, contracts, magic spells, surveys, dinner invitations, editions of literature believed wholly lost. Crates of papyrus from Oxyrhynchus poured into Oxford for decades, and scholars are still cataloguing and piecing together fragments by the hundred thousand; crowdsourced projects exist purely because no human lifetime suffices.

Out of that trash heap came entire comedies by Menander, the greatest playwright of Greek New Comedy, previously a rumor attached to quotations — including a play titled, perfectly, *The Grouch*. Out of it came fragments of gospels, of Euclid, of lyric poetry. Sappho's work, mostly annihilated by disuse and piety, keeps resurfacing partly through exactly this channel: her lines copied and recopied onto cheap sheets, then reused — folded into later books, pasted into mummy cartons, discarded to the dump — so that her voice, of all voices, arrives wrapped in other people's packaging. Fewer than seven hundred lines of her poetry survive, out of perhaps ten books' worth. Each new recovered fragment makes international news. Nobody in antiquity thought to preserve her; plenty of people thoughtlessly discarded the copies. Fortune chose the careless route.

* * *

My favorite of all these accidents involves a king who collected, a fire he couldn't prevent, and an unemployed engraver of banknotes.

In the seventh century BCE, the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembled at Nineveh the greatest library the world had seen — tens of thousands of clay tablets, including the accumulated masterpiece of Mesopotamian literature, the Epic of Gilgamesh, in twelve installments. When the empire collapsed and invaders burned the palaces in 612 BCE, the library suffered the worst fate clay knows: it got fired, hard, at temperature, forever. Sacking an enemy's palace turns out to be an excellent conservation technique if the holdings are ceramic. The ruins sat there, a jigsaw puzzle of baked碎 shards, until the nineteenth century, when excavators shipped mountains of fragments to the British Museum.

Enter George Smith, a working man self-taught in cuneiform, hired at the museum to sort the piles. In 1872, among tablets, he recognized a fragment recounting a global flood, a man forewarned, an ark, birds sent out to find land — centuries before Genesis was written. Witnesses describe him leaping up in wild excitement and, so the oft-repeated story goes, beginning to remove his clothing in disbelief. The announcement caused a public sensation that swept newspapers and pulpits alike. Realizing he possessed only part of the flood tablet, Smith hunted the missing pieces among the unsorted trays — and, astonishingly, found matching fragments sitting in the museum's own drawers. Funded by a newspaper, he raced to the site in Iraq and dug for more. He died at thirty-six of fever on the journey home, having given the Victorian world a jolt it never fully absorbed: deep time swallows our certainties, but sometimes hands back their precursors, perfectly cooked by catastrophe.

* * *

I think about the asymmetry involved in all this. For every Onfim, billions of minds passed through the world leaving not one trace — most humans who ever lived lived precisely before or outside writing, and within literate societies, the illiterate, the enslaved, the poor, and (much more often than not) women left the ground bare where a CV would go. The archive is a starlight model of the sky: bright points, vast dark between. Even the exceptions underline the rule; Claudia Severa's birthday invitation is precious precisely because a Roman woman's own hand is otherwise almost unheard of.

The ancients felt this void and invented a genre for it: letters to the dead. In Egypt, grieving families physically deposited written notes near tombs — petitions asking a departed father to intervene in a property dispute, a mother's plea about a sick child, instructions to stop hauntings. These letters survive in considerable numbers. Pause on that irony: the only mail guaranteed to be delivered was the mail addressed to no possible recipient, because we made sure to bury it. Everything written to the living went with the living. Impossibility was the precondition of permanence.

* * *

Which brings the discomfort home. Our era generates more text than all previous eras combined, and almost none of it is intended or structured to survive. Paper lasted; magnetic platters demagnetize. Clay tablets required fire to improve; solid-state drives quietly lose charge in a drawer. Institutional studies keep flagging "digital obsolescence" — formats unreadable within decades, media rotting in climate control. TheBBC's lavish 1986 interactive Domesday Project, built to mark 900 years of the actual eleventh-century Domesday Book (which remains perfectly legible on vellum), was itself almost unrecoverable within twenty years and needed emulation rescue efforts by teams of enthusiasts. We are, technologically speaking, writing on soap. Somewhere in the future, archaeologists may reconstruct twentieth-century life from bottle glass and landfills while finding the collected knowledge of the information age inexplicably absent — a dark-age silence backlit by laser discs that nobody's machine can play.

Maybe that is okay. Maybe the lesson cuts differently than anxiety. The things that reached us across all those centuries weren't urgent declarations, manifestos, or masterpieces of intent. They were habits. Alphabet practice. Grocery lists. Affectionate postscripts. Complaints about walls. Pressure of feet in wet ash. Nobody sharpened a point on eternity; eternity fell on the mundane the way ash falls on a morning. What persisted did so because it said *here I am, doing something small* — which turns out to be the most translatable sentence in any language.

* * *

So I keep coming back to Onfim, aged seven, dawdling over his alphabet in a birch forest town eight centuries ago, scribbling under an arithmetic drill the little prayer asking God to help his servant, sketching himself as a monster because monsters are more fun. He didn't know he was writing to us. Nobody told him. That's the secret economy of the whole business: he was writing to his afternoon, and we intercepted it.

If posterity ever recovers anything from any of us, odds are overwhelming that it will be some gesture of procedure rather than importance — a receipt, a doodle, a note reminding ourselves why we walked to the store. It comforts me more than it probably should. There is a strange democracy in this selection. Obscurity doesn't disqualify you; urgency doesn't qualify you. The mud takes volunteers regardless of rank, favoring those who wrote something true about smallness.

For what it's worth, across the distance: hello, Onfim. Your letters arrived. You have been heard.
